Theme

School & learning

superlative noun and adjective

degree of an adjective or adverb

also superlative degree, in the superlative, superlatives

classical

Quint. 1.5.45: per comparātiōnēs et superlātiōnēs
Charis. p. 88 P. (Lewis & Short)

superlātiō, superlātiōnis f.

noun, third declension

a superlative form

Quintilian’s word in grammar; in rhetoric the same word is hyperbole (Cic. de Or. 3.203).

Other words

  • superlātīvus, superlātīvī m. — the superlative degree

    noun, second declension · also used · late Latin · Charis. p. 87; Prisc. p. 605 P. (Lewis & Short); Traupman 232, 249

    The later grammarians’ gradus superlātīvus: doctissimus (Traupman 232). In the superlative is superlātīvē (Traupman 249): dīc «laetus» superlātīvē, give “laetus” in the superlative.

Examples

  • Dā gradum superlātīvum. — Longinquissimus.

    Give the superlative degree. — Most distant.Traupman 244

  • superlātīvē

    in the superlativeTraupman 388

  • Dīc “laetus” superlātīvē.

    Give me “laetus” in the superlative.Traupman 388

See also degree of comparison, comparative, adjective, most.

SourcesLewis & Short: superlatio · Lewis & Short: superlativus

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 232, 244, 249.
